transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-10-07 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Lucas Green (Redwood SE), Camille Rees (BlueCove Eng), Marcus Liu (BlueCove Product), Jenna Park (BlueCove SRE), Tomás Rivera (BlueCove CTO)

--- Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect) ---
Redwood walked through hosted API chat/generation basics: streaming chunking, election of generation params like temperature and top_p, stop sequences, token limits, and retries with jitter/backoff. Discussed concurrency tuning, continuous batching, and prefix/K V cache (transcribed K V cash in parts). Customer asked about latency SLOs under burst and compliance details; Redwood showed Console traces and Optimize recommendations.

[00:00] Ethan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — can you hear me?
[00:05] Camille: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:07] Marcus: Good to go.
[00:10] Ethan: Sweet. So the plan for today, we'll run through how the hosted API behaves for chat and generation, demo streaming, show how to tweak params and how retries and backoff work in practice, and then quick look at Console and Optimize recommendations. Priya will lead the deep bits.

[01:02] Priya: Hi all — I'm going to share my screen. One quick note, a lot of the demo traffic is synthetic so you may see slightly different latencies than your prod workload, but I'll point out which metrics map to which real world signals.

[02:15] Lucas: Also to flag, we'll show both client-side retry patterns and server-side fallbacks — e.g., if a larger variant is unavailable we'll fall back to a quantized variant with slightly different perf. Sometimes the transcript shows quantazeation, that's our internal shorthand.

[03:00] Camille: Before you dive in, two quick qualifiers from us — 1) our main use is conversational assistants within our analytics UI with lots of short messages, 2) we also batch long document summarization overnight. Our SRE cares about burst from peak dashboard loads; latency under 150ms for token streaming is a goal for UI feel.

[03:40] Priya: Great, that's helpful. For chat-first workloads we recommend smaller chunk sizes, streaming enabled, and low-latency routing. For long form summarization you can increase max_tokens and use batching/queueing with dedicated capacity if you need throughput.

[04:30] Marcus: Can you show streaming behavior? We want to know how partial tokens arrive and what a client can expect.

[04:55] Priya: Yep. Starting a streaming call now. Code sample: open websocket or use SDK streaming APIs; you get partial deltas in the same order as generation.

[05:40] [demo noise — screen share]
[06:05] Priya: (typing) here's a streaming response — you'll see first token chunk at 30–60ms depending on the generation step; subsequent chunks are more frequent. If you care about per-token latency we instrument in Console with token-level traces.

[07:10] Jenna: Are you measuring at the model step or including network hops?
[07:16] Priya: We include both; Console traces show breakdown: client→edge latency, model decode time, and edge batching wait time.

[08:00] Camille: What about retries? Our client currently does naive immediate retry on any error, which causes traffic spikes.

[08:20] Ethan: Good, we see that a lot. For retries we recommend exponential backoff with jitter, and a retry budget tied to idempotency — e.g., for generate calls that are not idempotent avoid blind retries without checking that the client can dedupe, or use an idempotency key.

[09:00] Priya: I'll demonstrate three patterns: client-side retry with exponential backoff + jitter, server-driven 429 with Retry-After, and offer for fallback routing to a cheaper quantized model.

[09:40] [09:40] Priya: Example backoff config: initial 100ms, factor 2, jitter 0.1–0.3, cap 5s. Shown in sample SDK call in the repo link: https://samples.redwood.ai/retries

[10:25] Marcus: If the first request partially succeeded and client retries, how do you avoid duplicated chat messages?

[10:32] Priya: We recommend sequencing with message IDs and server-side dedupe where possible. For full determinism send an idempotency token so the server knows if it already completed. In hosted mode we store short-lived request metadata for dedupe within a window.

[11:15] Tomás: What about streaming interruptions — if a connection drops in the middle of a generation can we resume?

[11:25] Lucas: Resumption semantics depend on whether you kept the KV cache. For short sessions the client can reconnect and ask for the last model state if you persist the session; but most customers do a quick replay from the last acknowledged message. We don't expose arbitrary continuation of a partially emitted sequence over the hosted API today.

[12:10] Camille: You mentioned prefix caching earlier — is that automatic?

[12:20] Priya: There are two layers: automatic prefix/K V cache for recent prefixes at the edge that speeds up autoregressive steps, and explicit session cache you can control. In the Console we show cache hit rate per route. Note — transcription sometimes shows K V cash.

[13:05] Marcus: Walk me through tuning generation parameters — temp, top_p, max_tokens, stop — and their UX tradeoffs.

[13:20] Priya: Sure. Temperature increases randomness; top_p controls nucleus sampling. For deterministic assistant responses use low temp (0–0.2) and maybe top_p ~0.9; for creative generation raise temp. max_tokens bounds the output. Stop tokens lower turnaround but be careful with multi-token stops.

[14:15] Priya: Live example — temp 0.0 vs 0.7 on the same prompt. We'll show the generated deltas streaming and how Console highlights token distributions.

[15:00] [15:00] Demo: short prompt with temp 0 → output is concise and repeats predictable phrasing. temp 0.7 → output has more varied synonyms.

[16:05] Jenna: For our UI we want predictable ends so stop tokens are important. Any gotchas?

[16:12] Priya: Yes — stop matching is exact; if you rely on punctuation only it can mismatch. Also watch truncation: if you hit token cap, generation stops abruptly — Console exposes model tokens used and a token_exhausted flag.

[17:00] Camille: How do you recommend batching for our overnight summarization? We currently push 10k docs in parallel and pay a lot for small overheads.

[17:20] Lucas: Use Redwood Optimize suggestions: combine documents into larger batches respecting max_input_tokens and use our batch endpoint where the runtime does continuous batching. For hosted you can tune concurrency and set a target latency SLO; Optimize will recommend a batching window that reduces cost while keeping latency acceptable.

[18:15] Marcus: Any quick math you can share for token cost vs latency tradeoffs?

[18:28] Priya: A rule of thumb: increasing batch size reduces per-token compute overhead by ~10–30% depending on model, but increases tail latency. We'll share a spreadsheet with sample numbers and model profiles.

[19:02] Tomás: On security — we need SOC2 attestations and KMS integration.

[19:10] Ethan: We are SOC 2 Type II and support customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated; hosted customers can use our managed KMS but we also provide audit logs and SSO/SAML. We'll send the compliance bundle.

[20:05] Jenna: Are logs redacted? Are full input strings retained?

[20:12] Ethan: By default hosted stores request logs short-term; you can configure retention and opt-out of storing user content, or use Private which keeps everything on your VPC. Audit logs contain operation metadata, not always full user text unless enabled.

[21:00] Priya: Back to retries and fallbacks — I'll simulate a 429 burst and show how client backoff + server Retry-After behaves.

[21:45] [21:45] Demo: firing a burst of parallel requests. Initially some calls succeed, then 429 responses with Retry-After: 1200ms appear. Client respect results in smoothing the traffic.

[22:50] Marcus: If we get a 503 due to a model oom, do you fallback automatically?

[23:00] Lucas: We have automatic fallback policies: route to a compatible quantized or smaller variant if configured. For some customers we set a route-level fallback to a cheaper model during periods of constrained capacity. That is configurable via the Console rollout rules.

[24:05] Camille: Can you demo the Console trace that shows where time is spent?

[24:20] Priya: Screen share — here is a request trace: client→edge (12ms), waiting in batch queue (45ms), model decode (60ms), streaming first chunk (32ms). You can drill into token-level slices.

[25:40] Marcus: How about observability for cost — can we see per-route cost and token breakdown by user?

[25:55] Ethan: Yep — Console shows per-route cost, token counts, and you can tag tokens by project or user. We also provide token-level cost attribution in our billing exports.

[26:30] Jenna: For network SRE, we have spikes on 75th percentile during reports takedown; what are recommended settings to avoid cascading retries?

[26:45] Priya: Use a retry budget pattern on the client side: limit retries per time window per user, use server Retry-After headers, and for heavy bursts move to a dedicated pool if predictable. Also consider rate-limiting at the edge with graceful 429 responses.

[27:30] Marcus: In terms of SDKs, do you provide builtin retry logic?

[27:35] Ethan: Yes — our SDKs include configurable retry policies with sensible defaults and built-in jitter. You can override them. We'll send code examples.

[28:10] Camille: On cost controls, any quick levers?

[28:15] Priya: Model routing (cheaper fallback models), token limit enforcement, caching of common prefixes, and Optimize's quantization recommendations. Also per-route quotas and alerts in Console.

[29:05] Tomás: We have a question about deterministic outputs for some analytics — is temperature 0 enough?

[29:12] Priya: Setting temp=0 greatly reduces randomness but non-determinism can still arise from sampling in some architectures. For strict determinism we recommend deterministic decoding or using logit bias and low temperature plus model version pinning.

[30:10] [30:10] Demo: we flip model versions in Console — showing a canary rollout to 10% traffic then to 100% with automatic rollback if error rate spikes.

[31:05] Marcus: How do you handle schema for function/tool calls in streaming?

[31:20] Priya: We stream tool call partials as structured deltas and mark tool boundaries; client can detect a function call start and then buffer arguments. The SDK has helpers to parse and surface partial tool outputs.

[32:40] Camille: Are there any gotchas when using stop tokens with tool calls?

[32:50] Lucas: Stop tokens can truncate the tool call payload if not carefully chosen. We recommend delimiting tool outputs with explicit markers and validating on the client side.

[33:30] Marcus: Let's talk about the pilot — what do you need from us to run a realistic 72-hour concurrency benchmark?

[33:45] Ethan: Sample traffic shapes, expected peak rps, typical prompt sizes, and success criteria (latency p95, cost per 1k tokens). Priya will provide a lightweight script and we'll run it under a test project with telemetry shared to your team.

[34:30] Priya: I'll also include a variant that toggles caching and batching so you can see differences.

[35:12] Jenna: On networking we use private subnets — is private deployment mandatory for compliance?

[35:22] Ethan: Not mandatory — hosted can meet many compliance needs with audit logs and encryption, but for customer-managed keys or air-gapped requirements, Private or Dedicated are better. We'll outline tradeoffs in the security bundle.

[36:10] Marcus: Any constraints on token limits per request?

[36:18] Priya: We support up to model-specific token caps; for our bigger variants it's currently ~32k context for certain models. If you need more we can discuss sharding prompts or session-level KV cache.

[37:05] Camille: Show us an example SDK call with backoff config and idempotency key.

[37:20] Lucas: (reads code aloud) simple: client.generate({prompt, idempotency_key: uuid, retry_policy: {initial_ms:100, factor:2, jitter:0.2, max_attempts:5}}) — that pattern avoids hot loops.

[38:40] Marcus: On billing, can you show a typical cost breakdown for a chat-heavy workload?

[38:55] Ethan: We'll share a sample billing export. Rough split: 60% model compute, 25% token egress, 15% infra overhead; caching reduces compute.

[40:10] Camille: For long-term monitoring we want regression alerts when quality drops. Does Optimize help?

[40:20] Priya: Yes — Redwood Optimize can track eval sets and prompt-based regressions, tie them to rollouts, and raise alerts if quality drops after a model change. It can also suggest quantization changes to save cost with minimal quality loss.

[41:00] Tomás: Any latency SLOs you commit to on hosted?

[41:10] Ethan: Hosted doesn't have the same SLA as Dedicated, but we publish verified profiles and typical p95 numbers per model and region; Dedicated offers SLA-backed latency guarantees. We'll point you to the performance pages.

[42:05] Marcus: If we need burst capacity occasionally, can we combine Dedicated and Hosted?

[42:15] Priya: Yes — customers use a hybrid approach: Dedicated for baseline traffic and Hosted for burst overflow; Smart routing can spill traffic to hosted in configured policies.

[43:00] Camille: Any final caveats about streaming for mobile clients?

[43:10] Lucas: For mobile, unstable networks might need smaller chunks, more aggressive timeouts, and good retry budgets. Consider sending smaller prompts to reduce re-sends.

[44:05] Marcus: OK — let's recap next steps.

[44:12] Ethan: Recap: Redwood will send sample SDK snippets and backoff configs, a benchmarking script, Console screenshots (cache/hit rates and traces), and compliance bundle. BlueCove will share traffic shapes and success criteria and we'll schedule the 72-hour pilot kickoff next week.

[45:00] Camille: Sounds good. Marcus and Jenna will coordinate the network details.

[46:10] Tomás: One quick ask — can you include sample guardrails for stop tokens and tool call validation?

[46:20] Priya: Yes — we'll add that to the follow-up pack.

[47:00] Ethan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with the artifacts. End call.
